mathprize-2026-01.title: Vieta
mathprize-2026-01.body:
A non-vertical line through $(3,10)$ is $y=m(x-3)+10$ (a vertical line meets the parabola only once). Intersecting with $y=x^2$: $x^2-mx+3m-10=0$, whose discriminant $m^2-12m+40=(m-6)^2+4$ is always positive. By Vieta, $x_1+x_2=m$ and $x_1x_2=3m-10$, so
$$y_1+y_2=x_1^2+x_2^2=m^2-2(3m-10)=(m-3)^2+11\ge11,$$
with equality for $m=3$.

**Answer: 11**

mathprize-2026-01.title: Check the optimal line
mathprize-2026-01.body:
For $m=3$ the line is $y=3x+1$, meeting $y=x^2$ where $x^2-3x-1=0$: $x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}$. Then $x_1^2+x_2^2=(x_1+x_2)^2-2x_1x_2=9+2=11$. Any other slope adds $(m-3)^2>0$.

**Answer: 11**

mathprize-2026-02.title: The pattern repeats every two steps
mathprize-2026-02.body:
$S_1=[0,1]^2$ and $R_1=[0,1]\times[0,\frac12]$. The top half $[0,1]\times[\frac12,1]$ rotated $90^\circ$ clockwise about $(1,\frac12)$ is $S_2=[1,\frac32]\times[\frac12,\frac32]$, so $R_2=[1,\frac32]\times[\frac12,1]$. Its top half $[1,\frac32]\times[1,\frac32]$ rotated about $(\frac32,1)$ gives $S_3=[\frac32,2]\times[1,\frac32]$, a square of side $\frac12$.

So $S_3$ is $S_1$ scaled by $\frac12$ with bottom-left corner $(\frac32,1)$; in general $S_{2k+1}$ is a square of side $2^{-k}$ with bottom-left corner $(3,2)(1-2^{-k})$ — all on the line $y=\frac23x$. The map taking $S_1$ to $S_3$ is a homothety centered at $(3,2)$ on that line, so it preserves the line, and each pair $R_{2k+1},R_{2k+2}$ has the same fraction of its area below the line as $R_1,R_2$.

- $R_1$ (area $\frac12$): the part above the line is $\{x<\frac{3y}{2}\}$, of area $\int_0^{1/2}\frac{3y}{2}dy=\frac3{16}$; below: $\frac5{16}$.
- $R_2$ (area $\frac14$): below the line means $\frac12\le y\le\frac{2x}{3}$, area $\int_1^{3/2}\left(\frac{2x}3-\frac12\right)dx=\frac{5}{12}-\frac14=\frac16$.

Fraction: $\dfrac{\frac5{16}+\frac16}{\frac34}=\dfrac{23/48}{3/4}=\dfrac{23}{36}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{36}$**

mathprize-2026-02.title: Exact computation
mathprize-2026-02.body:
Generating $R_1,\dots,R_{80}$ with exact rational coordinates (following the rotation rule) and clipping each against the half-plane $3y\le2x$, the ratio of the area below the line to the total area converges to $0.638888\ldots=\frac{23}{36}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{36}$**

mathprize-2026-03.title: Count reduced fractions
mathprize-2026-03.body:
For $P=(x,y)$, $\tan\angle POX=\frac yx$ and $\tan\angle POY=\frac xy$, so the element is $r+\frac1r$ with $r=\frac yx$. Since $r+\frac1r=s+\frac1s$ iff $s=r$ or $s=\frac1r$, the size of $S$ is the number of distinct ratios $r\le1$, i.e. reduced fractions $\frac pq$ with $1\le p\le q\le12$:
$$1+\sum_{q=2}^{12}\varphi(q)=1+(1+2+2+4+2+6+4+6+4+10+4)=46.$$

**Answer: 46**

mathprize-2026-03.title: Brute force
mathprize-2026-03.body:
Computing $\frac yx+\frac xy$ as exact fractions for all $144$ points and counting distinct values gives $46$.

**Answer: 46**

mathprize-2026-04.title: Optimize a chord sum
mathprize-2026-04.body:
Put the branch point at the origin, the line along the $x$-axis and the ray along the positive $y$-axis; let the center be $(a,b)$.

The line contributes the chord $2\sqrt{100-b^2}$. The $y$-axis meets the disk in $[\,b-\sqrt{100-a^2},\,b+\sqrt{100-a^2}\,]$, and only the part with $y\ge0$ counts; for fixed $b$ this shrinks as $|a|$ grows, so $a=0$. With $a=0$ and $0\le b<10$, the ray contributes $b+10$, so we maximize
$$f(b)=2\sqrt{100-b^2}+b+10.$$
$f'(b)=1-\frac{2b}{\sqrt{100-b^2}}=0\iff 100-b^2=4b^2\iff b^2=20$. (Negative $b$ is worse, as the ray part is then $10+b<10$.) The maximum length is $8\sqrt5+2\sqrt5+10=10\sqrt5+10$, and the squared distance from the center $(0,\sqrt{20})$ to the branch point is $20$.

**Answer: 20**

mathprize-2026-04.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
mathprize-2026-04.body:
With $a=0$ (as argued) we maximize $2\sqrt{100-b^2}+b$. By Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$2\sqrt{100-b^2}+1\cdot b\le\sqrt{(2^2+1^2)\big((100-b^2)+b^2\big)}=\sqrt{500}=10\sqrt5,$$
with equality when $\frac{\sqrt{100-b^2}}{2}=\frac{b}{1}$, i.e. $b^2=20$. So the squared distance is $a^2+b^2=20$. (A numerical optimization over $(a,b)$ agrees.)

**Answer: 20**

mathprize-2026-05.title: Intersections are inversions
mathprize-2026-05.body:
Lines $j<k$ meet where $m_jx+j=m_kx+k$, i.e. $x=\frac{k-j}{m_j-m_k}$, which is positive iff $m_j>m_k$. (With probability $1$ the slopes are distinct and no three lines are concurrent, so intersections are distinct points.) So the number of intersections with $x>0$ is the number of **inversions** of the sequence $m_1,\dots,m_7$.

The relative order of the $m_k$ is a uniformly random permutation of $7$ elements. Permutations with exactly $2$ inversions: either two disjoint adjacent transpositions, or a pattern like $231$/$312$ on three consecutive positions. Count: $\binom{6}{2}-5=10$ ways to pick two non-overlapping adjacent swaps (out of the $6$ adjacent positions, excluding the $5$ overlapping pairs), plus $2\cdot5=10$ three-element rotations: $20$ in total. (In general the number is $\frac{(n-2)(n+1)}{2}$.)

Probability $\frac{20}{7!}=\frac{20}{5040}=\frac1{252}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{252}$**

mathprize-2026-05.title: Enumerate permutations
mathprize-2026-05.body:
Looping over all $5040$ permutations of $7$ and counting those with exactly $2$ inversions gives $20$. So the probability is $\frac{20}{5040}=\frac1{252}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{252}$**

mathprize-2026-06.title: Count points on a conic
mathprize-2026-06.body:
Work in $\mathbb F_{101}$; the condition is $a,b,c\ne0$ and $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

**All solutions in $\mathbb F_p^3$.** For $c\ne0$, scaling gives $(a/c)^2+(b/c)^2=1$, a circle with $p-1$ points when $p\equiv1\pmod4$ (parametrize by lines through $(-1,0)$; the two slopes $\pm i$ give no new point). So there are $(p-1)^2$ solutions with $c\ne0$, plus those with $c=0$: $a^2+b^2=0$, i.e. $b=\pm ia$, giving $2(p-1)+1=2p-1$. Total $p^2-2p+1+2p-1=p^2$.

**Remove zeros.** $a=0$: $b=\pm c$, $2p-1$ solutions; likewise $b=0$ and $c=0$: $2p-1$ each. Two coordinates zero forces the third zero. By inclusion–exclusion the solutions with some zero coordinate number $3(2p-1)-3+1=6p-5$.

So the count is $p^2-6p+5=(p-1)(p-5)=100\cdot96=9600$.

**Answer: 9600**

mathprize-2026-06.title: Brute force
mathprize-2026-06.body:
Checking all $100^3$ triples by computer gives $9600$ solutions.

**Answer: 9600**

mathprize-2026-07.title: Orthic triangle of $BCD$
mathprize-2026-07.body:
Since $\angle B\ne\angle D$, the axis of the kite is $BD$: $BA=BC$, $DA=DC$, and $A$, $C$ are mirror images in $BD$. So $AC\perp BD$ at $O$. Triangle $BCD$ has angles $\angle CBD=80^\circ$, $\angle BDC=65^\circ$, $\angle BCD=35^\circ$ (acute).

In triangle $BCD$, $O$ is the foot of the altitude from $C$ and $F$ the foot from $B$. Let $H$ be the foot from $D$ on $BC$. In the orthic triangle $OFH$, the altitude $CO$ bisects the angle at $O$; since $BD\perp CO$, the lines $OF$ and $OH$ are mirror images in $BD$. Reflecting in $BD$ sends line $BC$ to line $BA$ and $H$ to the foot $H'$ of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AB$; and $H'$ lies on the reflection of $OH$, which is $OF$. Hence $G=H'$: $G$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AB$.

Now reflect back: $\angle FGD=\angle OGD=\angle OHD$. At the foot $H$ the orthic angle is $180^\circ-2\angle BDC=50^\circ$, bisected by the altitude $HD$, so $\angle OHD=25^\circ$. Therefore $t=25$.

**Answer: 25**

mathprize-2026-07.title: Coordinates
mathprize-2026-07.body:
Take $B=(0,0)$ with $BD$ along the positive $x$-axis and $BA=BC=1$: $A=(\cos80^\circ,\sin80^\circ)$, $C=(\cos80^\circ,-\sin80^\circ)$, $O=(\cos80^\circ,0)$, and $D$ on the $x$-axis with $\angle ADB=65^\circ$: $D\approx(0.6329,0)$. Then $F$, the foot from $B$ on $CD$, is $\approx(0.5198,-0.2424)$ and $G=AB\cap OF\approx(0.0191,0.1082)$. Computing the angle between $\vec{GF}$ and $\vec{GD}$ gives $25.000^\circ$ (and $\angle AGD=90^\circ$, confirming $G$ is the foot from $D$).

**Answer: 25**

mathprize-2026-08.title: Central projection
mathprize-2026-08.body:
Let the light be $L=(x_0,y_0,z_0)$. A point $(0,y,z)$ projects from $L$ to the plane $z=0$ at parameter $\tau=\frac{z_0}{z_0-z}$ along $L\to P$:
$$\left(x_0(1-\tau),\ y_0+\tau(y-y_0)\right),\qquad 1-\tau=\frac{-z}{z_0-z}.$$
The parallel sides of the trapezoid (at $z=80$, length $16$, and $z=75$, length $18$) project to segments parallel to the $y$-axis, of lengths $16\tau_{80}$ and $18\tau_{75}$. For a square these are equal:
$$\frac{16z_0}{z_0-80}=\frac{18z_0}{z_0-75}\ \Rightarrow\ 16(z_0-75)=18(z_0-80)\ \Rightarrow\ z_0=120.$$
Then $\tau_{80}=3$, $\tau_{75}=\frac83$ and the side is $48$. The two images lie at $x$-coordinates $x_0(1-3)=-2x_0$ and $x_0(1-\frac83)=-\frac53x_0$, which are $\frac{x_0}{3}$ apart, so $\frac{x_0}3=48$ and $x_0=144$.

(The other sides are parallel to the $x$-axis when $y_0+3(56-y_0)=y_0+\frac83(51-y_0)$, i.e. $y_0=96$; then the $y$-ranges are $[24,72]$ for both.)

**Answer: 144**

mathprize-2026-09.title: Recognize $(z+1)^8-z^8$
mathprize-2026-09.body:
The coefficients are $\binom8k$ for $k\le7$, so the polynomial is $(z+1)^8-z^8$. Its roots satisfy $\left(\frac{z+1}{z}\right)^8=1$, i.e. $1+\frac1z=\omega$ with $\omega=e^{i\theta}$, $\theta=\frac{2\pi k}{8}$, $k=1,\dots,7$. Then
$$z=\frac{1}{e^{i\theta}-1}=\frac{e^{-i\theta/2}}{2i\sin(\theta/2)}=-\frac12-\frac i2\cot\frac\theta2.$$
The imaginary part $-\frac12\cot\frac\theta2$ is largest when $\frac\theta2=\frac{7\pi}{8}$: $-\frac12\cot\frac{7\pi}8=\frac12\cot\frac\pi8=\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac12+\frac12\sqrt2$**

mathprize-2026-09.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2026-09.body:
All roots have real part $-\frac12$ (they are the points equidistant from $0$ and $-1$, since $|z+1|=|z|$). Numerically the roots' imaginary parts are $\pm0.2071,\pm0.5,\pm1.2071$ and $0$; the largest is $1.2071\ldots=\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac12+\frac12\sqrt2$**

mathprize-2026-10.title: Three angles summing to $0$
mathprize-2026-10.body:
Let $x=t^\circ$, $y=7t^\circ$, $z=-8t^\circ$, so $x+y+z=0$ and the expression is $-(\sin x+\sin y+\sin z)$.

Write the expression as $E=\sin(x+y)-\sin x-\sin y$ and put $u=\frac{x+y}{2}$, $v=\frac{x-y}{2}$:
$$E=2\sin u\cos u-2\sin u\cos v=2\sin u\,(\cos u-\cos v).$$
For fixed $u$ the best choice is $\cos v=-1$ if $\sin u>0$ (giving $2\sin u(1+\cos u)$) or $\cos v=1$ if $\sin u<0$ (giving $2|\sin u|(1-\cos u)$). Maximizing $h(u)=2\sin u(1+\cos u)$ on $(0^\circ,180^\circ)$: $h'(u)=2\cos u+2\cos2u=0$ gives $\cos u=\frac12$, $u=60^\circ$, $h=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac32=\frac{3\sqrt3}2$; the other branch is the same by $u\mapsto u+180^\circ$. In every equality case $x=u+v$ and $y=u-v$ are both $\equiv240^\circ\pmod{360^\circ}$.

So the maximum $\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$ requires $t\equiv240$ and $7t\equiv240\pmod{360}$, i.e. $t\equiv240\pmod{360}$ (then $7t=1680\equiv240$ ✓). The smallest positive such $t$ is $240$. Check: $\sin1920^\circ=\sin120^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $-\sin240^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $-\sin1680^\circ=-\sin240^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$: total $\frac{3\sqrt3}2$.

**Answer: 240**

mathprize-2026-10.title: Numerical search
mathprize-2026-10.body:
Evaluating the expression for $t\in[0,360]$ on a grid of step $10^{-4}$ (it has period $360$), the maximum value $2.598076\ldots=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$ is attained only near $t=240$, so the smallest positive maximizer is $t=240$.

**Answer: 240**

mathprize-2026-11.title: Direct computation
mathprize-2026-11.body:
$\binom{132}{4}=12082785$ and $\binom{190}{4}=52602165$, with sum $64684950$. And $\binom{200}{4}=\frac{200\cdot199\cdot198\cdot197}{24}=64684950$. Since $\binom n4$ is increasing in $n\ge4$, $n=200$ is the only solution.

**Answer: 200**

mathprize-2026-12.title: Parity and a small Markov chain
mathprize-2026-12.body:
The streets form the graph with top row $A-\star-E$, bottom row $B-C-D$ and verticals $A-B$, $\star-C$, $E-D$. Each walker moves to a uniformly random neighbor every step.

**No ties.** Color the corners like a checkerboard: $A,C,E$ white and $B,\star,D$ black. Every step changes color, and Ally starts on white, Bea on black. So Ally can only be at $\star$ after an odd number of steps and Bea after an even number: they never arrive simultaneously.

**Reduce by symmetry.** Classify corners: $X=\{A,E\}$ (next to $\star$), $Y=\{B,D\}$, $Z=\{C\}$. From $X$: $\star$ or $Y$ with probability $\frac12$ each; from $Y$: $X$ or $Z$, $\frac12$ each; from $Z$: $\star$ with $\frac13$, $Y$ with $\frac23$. Let $p_{UV}$ be Ally's winning probability with Ally in class $U$, Bea in class $V$ (both about to move). By parity the states are $XY, ZY$ (Ally to move from $X$ or $Z$; Bea can't reach $\star$ this step) and $YX, YZ$ (Ally can't reach $\star$):
$$p_{XY}=\tfrac12+\tfrac12w,\quad p_{ZY}=\tfrac13+\tfrac23w,\quad p_{YX}=\tfrac12u,\quad p_{YZ}=\tfrac23u,$$
where $u=\frac{p_{XY}+p_{ZY}}{2}$ and $w=\frac{p_{YX}+p_{YZ}}{2}$ (the other walker lands in each of its two classes with probability $\frac12$). Then $w=\frac12\left(\frac u2+\frac{2u}3\right)=\frac{7u}{12}$ and $u=\frac12\left(\frac56+\frac76w\right)=\frac5{12}+\frac{7w}{12}$. So $u=\frac5{12}+\frac{49u}{144}$, $u=\frac{12}{19}$, $w=\frac7{19}$, and
$$p_{XY}=\frac12+\frac{7}{38}=\frac{13}{19}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{13}{19}$**

mathprize-2026-12.title: Full chain and simulation
mathprize-2026-12.body:
Solving the linear system for all $25$ joint positions (neither at $\star$) with exact fractions gives $\frac{13}{19}$ from $(A,B)$; a simulation of $400{,}000$ games gives $0.684\approx\frac{13}{19}=0.6842$, and no game ends in a tie.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{19}$**

mathprize-2026-13.title: Farey neighbors
mathprize-2026-13.body:
Let $r=\frac1c$. Every line through the origin meets the circle at the origin, so we need every line through $O$ to come within distance $r$ of some other lattice point $(p,q)$ of the box. By symmetry consider directions with slope $s\in[0,1]$.

Between two consecutive fractions $\frac ab<\frac{a'}{b'}$ of the Farey sequence of order $22$ (so $a'b-ab'=1$), the distance from the line of slope $s$ to $(b,a)$ grows and the distance to $(b',a')$ shrinks as $s$ increases, and they are equal on the line through the "mediant" point $(b+b',a+a')$, where both distances equal $\frac{1}{\sqrt{(b+b')^2+(a+a')^2}}$. No lattice point of the box is closer to that line: for any $(p,q)$, the distance is $\frac{|p(a+a')-q(b+b')|}{\sqrt{(b+b')^2+(a+a')^2}}$ with a nonzero integer numerator (as $b+b'>22$ and the mediant is reduced). So the worst line in that gap has nearest distance exactly $\frac1{\sqrt{(b+b')^2+(a+a')^2}}$.

The largest such distance comes from the smallest mediant vector. Consecutive Farey fractions of order $22$ have $b+b'\ge23$, and the gap $\frac01,\frac1{22}$ gives the mediant $(23,1)$ with $23^2+1^2=530$, the smallest possible. So we need $r\ge\frac{1}{\sqrt{530}}$, and this suffices. Hence $c_{\max}=\sqrt{530}$ ($530=2\cdot5\cdot53$ is square-free).

**Answer: $\sqrt{530}$**

mathprize-2026-13.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2026-13.body:
Scanning $400{,}001$ directions $\theta\in[0^\circ,45^\circ]$ and computing the distance from the line to the nearest of the $2024$ nonzero lattice points, the largest such distance is $0.04343\ldots$ at $\theta\approx2.49^\circ$ ($\tan\theta\approx\frac1{23}$), i.e. $\frac1{\sqrt{530}}=0.043437$. So $c=\sqrt{530}\approx23.02$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{530}$**

mathprize-2026-14.title: Telescoping with $F_{n+6}-F_n=4F_{n+3}$
mathprize-2026-14.body:
First, $F_{n+6}-F_n=4F_{n+3}$: indeed $F_{n+6}=3F_{n+3}+2F_{n+2}$ and $F_n=F_{n+2}-F_{n+1}=2F_{n+2}-F_{n+3}$.

Let $u_n=\frac{1}{F_nF_{n+1}F_{n+2}F_{n+3}F_{n+4}F_{n+5}}$. Then
$$u_n-u_{n+1}=\frac{F_{n+6}-F_n}{F_nF_{n+1}\cdots F_{n+6}}=\frac{4F_{n+3}}{F_n\cdots F_{n+6}}=\frac{4}{F_nF_{n+1}F_{n+2}F_{n+4}F_{n+5}F_{n+6}}.$$
So the sum telescopes to $\frac14u_1=\frac{1}{4\cdot F_1F_2F_3F_4F_5F_6}=\frac{1}{4\cdot1\cdot1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot8}=\frac1{960}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{960}$**

mathprize-2026-14.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2026-14.body:
The terms decrease very fast: $\frac{1}{1\cdot1\cdot2\cdot5\cdot8\cdot13}=\frac1{1040}$, then $\frac1{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot8\cdot13\cdot21}=\frac{1}{13104}$, etc. Summing $300$ terms with $50$-digit precision gives $0.00104166666\ldots=\frac1{960}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{960}$**

mathprize-2026-15.title: A line in the $bc$-plane
mathprize-2026-15.body:
A number $r$ is a root of $x^2-bx+c$ iff $c=br-r^2$, i.e. the point $(b,c)$ lies on the line $\ell_r: rb-c-r^2=0$. So $r$ occurs as a root iff $\ell_r$ meets the disk of radius $\sqrt{512}$ centered at $(-18,-15)$:
$$\frac{|{-18r}+15-r^2|}{\sqrt{r^2+1}}\le\sqrt{512}\iff (r^2+18r-15)^2\le512(r^2+1).$$
At $r=7$: $(49+126-15)^2=160^2=25600=512\cdot50$ — equality. For $r>7$ the left side grows like $r^4$ faster than the right side (the difference $h(r)=(r^2+18r-15)^2-512(r^2+1)$ has $h(7)=0$ and $h'(r)=2(r^2+18r-15)(2r+18)-1024r>0$ for $r\ge7$). So the largest root is $7$, attained at the tangent point $(b,c)=(-18,-15)+\frac{\sqrt{512}}{\sqrt{50}}(7,-1)=\left(\frac{22}{5},-\frac{91}{5}\right)$, which gives $x^2-\frac{22}5x-\frac{91}5=(x-7)\left(x+\frac{13}5\right)$.

**Answer: 7**

mathprize-2026-15.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2026-15.body:
Parametrize the boundary circle $b=-18+\sqrt{512}\cos\phi$, $c=-15+\sqrt{512}\sin\phi$ (the largest root is attained on the boundary, since increasing $b$ or decreasing $c$ increases $\frac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4c}}{2}$). Maximizing $\frac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4c}}2$ over $\phi$ numerically gives $6.9999999\ldots$, i.e. $7$.

**Answer: 7**

mathprize-2026-16.title: Telescoping arctangents
mathprize-2026-16.body:
Look for $\arctan u-\arctan v=\arctan\frac{u-v}{1+uv}$ with $u-v=8n$, $1+uv=16n^4+5$. Then $uv=16n^4+4=(4n^2+2)^2-16n^2=(4n^2+4n+2)(4n^2-4n+2)$, and indeed $u=4n^2+4n+2$, $v=4n^2-4n+2$ differ by $8n$. Note $u=(2n+1)^2+1$ and $v=(2n-1)^2+1$. So with $g(m)=\arctan(m^2+1)$,
$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}\arctan\frac{8n}{16n^4+5}=\sum_{n=1}^N\big(g(2n+1)-g(2n-1)\big)=g(2N+1)-g(1)\to\frac\pi2-\arctan2.$$
Hence $\tan s=\cot(\arctan2)=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

mathprize-2026-16.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2026-16.body:
Summing $200{,}000$ terms gives $s\approx0.4636476$, which is $\arctan\frac12$; so $\tan s=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

mathprize-2026-17.title: Angles from the icosahedron's axes
mathprize-2026-17.body:
Opposite vertices give the same great circle, so there are $6$ great circles, one per diagonal of the icosahedron. Any two of the $6$ diagonals meet at the same angle $\alpha$ with $\cos\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt5}$ (e.g. the vertices $(0,\pm1,\pm\varphi)$: $\frac{(0,1,\varphi)\cdot(0,-1,\varphi)}{1+\varphi^2}=\frac{\varphi^2-1}{\varphi^2+1}=\frac{\varphi}{\varphi+2}=\frac1{\sqrt5}$). Two great circles cross at the angle between their poles, so at every crossing the four angles are $\alpha$ and $\pi-\alpha$ ($\alpha\approx63.43^\circ$).

The $6$ circles meet in $\binom62\cdot2=30$ points, each on $2$ circles, so there are $60$ edges and, by Euler, $32$ faces: $20$ triangles and $12$ pentagons (the icosidodecahedral pattern), alternating around each vertex. The triangles have the acute angles $\alpha$ (area $3\alpha-\pi\approx0.18$) and the pentagons the obtuse angles $\pi-\alpha$, so by Girard's theorem
$$A=5(\pi-\alpha)-3\pi=2\pi-5\alpha,\qquad\cos A=\cos5\alpha.$$
(Check: $20(3\alpha-\pi)+12(2\pi-5\alpha)=4\pi$. ✓) With $c=\cos\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt5}$, $\cos5\alpha=16c^5-20c^3+5c=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\left(\frac{16}{25}-4+5\right)=\frac{41}{25\sqrt5}=\frac{41\sqrt5}{125}$.

**Answer: $\frac{41\sqrt5}{125}$**

mathprize-2026-17.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2026-17.body:
Building the $6$ great circles from the icosahedron's vertices, computing all $30$ crossing points, and grouping random points by their sign pattern gives $32$ faces: $20$ triangles and $12$ pentagons. For a pentagon, summing the vertex angles and subtracting $3\pi$ gives $A\approx0.747442$, and $\cos A\approx0.733430=\frac{41\sqrt5}{125}$.

**Answer: $\frac{41\sqrt5}{125}$**

mathprize-2026-18.title: Exact computation
mathprize-2026-18.body:
Computing $M^{1000}(1,0,1)^T$ with exact integer arithmetic (repeated squaring) gives top entry $20008001$, matching the binomial formula.

**Answer: 20008001**

mathprize-2026-19.title: Insert the caramels
mathprize-2026-19.body:
Each row holds one type, so an eating order is just a word with four each of $a,b,c$ and no two equal adjacent letters.

Take the word in $a,b$ alone (delete the $c$'s). If it has $r$ runs, it has $8-r$ adjacent equal pairs, and each must be separated by a $c$; the $c$'s must go into distinct gaps (no two adjacent). So $r\ge4$, and the remaining $4-(8-r)=r-4$ $c$'s go into the other $r+1$ gaps (between runs or at the ends): $\binom{r+1}{r-4}$ ways.

The number of $a,b$ words (four each) with $r$ runs is $2\binom3{k-1}^2$ for $r=2k$ and $2\binom3k\binom3{k-1}$ for $r=2k+1$:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} r&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline \text{words}&18&18&18&6&2\\ \binom{r+1}{r-4}&1&6&21&56&126\end{array}$$
Total $18+108+378+336+252=1092$.

**Answer: 1092**

mathprize-2026-19.title: Recursion by computer
mathprize-2026-19.body:
Let $g(a,b,c,\ell)$ be the number of ways to finish with $a,b,c$ snacks left and last type $\ell$; $g(0,0,0,\ell)=1$ and $g$ sums over the types $\ne\ell$ still available. Evaluating $g(4,4,4,\text{none})$ gives $1092$.

**Answer: 1092**

mathprize-2026-20.title: Linear maps and the best cycle
mathprize-2026-20.body:
Track $(A,B,P)$, where $P$ is the A-income still owed "right after the next turn". The two moves are linear:
$$\text{(1) }(A,B,P)\mapsto(A+P,\ B+\tfrac A4,\ 0),\qquad \text{(2) }(A,B,P)\mapsto(A+B+P,\ B,\ B),$$
with matrices $M_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\\frac14&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $M_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Everything is nonnegative and monotone, so $a_n$ is the largest first coordinate over all products of $n$ matrices applied to $(1,1,0)$, and $\lim\sqrt[n]{a_n}$ is the joint growth rate of $\{M_1,M_2\}$.

Alternating in pairs, $1,1,2,2,1,1,2,2,\ldots$, is optimal (intuitively, it pays to convert in bursts: two moves of type (1) grow B, then two moves of type (2) collect both the immediate and the delayed A). The cycle matrix $T=M_2M_2M_1M_1$ has characteristic polynomial $\lambda(4\lambda^2-15\lambda+3)/4$, with largest eigenvalue
$$\lambda=\frac{15+\sqrt{177}}{8}\approx3.538,$$
so the growth rate is $\lambda^{1/4}=\sqrt[4]{\frac{15}{8}+\frac18\sqrt{177}}\approx1.37148$.

A dynamic program over all move sequences (keeping only non-dominated states $(A,B,P)$) confirms this: $(a_{60}/a_{40})^{1/20}=1.37148\ldots$, and an exhaustive search over all periodic patterns of length $\le12$ finds no cycle with a larger growth rate.

**Minimal $m+z$.** $\lambda^{1/4}$ is not of the form $\sqrt[m]{x+y\sqrt z}$ with $m<4$: e.g. $\sqrt\lambda=p+q\sqrt{177}$ would need $p^2+177q^2=\frac{15}8$, $2pq=\frac18$, i.e. $45312q^4-480q^2+1=0$, whose discriminant $49152=2^{14}\cdot3$ is not a square. With $m=4$, $x+y\sqrt z=\lambda$ forces $z=177$, and larger $m$ (such as $m=8$ with $\lambda^2$) do not reduce $z$. So the smallest value is $m+z=4+177=181$.

**Answer: 181**
